introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2024. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Question 8 : dates de l'historiographie courante (Quadruple Alliance de novembre 1815, congrès d'Aix-la-Chapelle 1818, de Troppau 1820, de Laybach 1821 et de Vérone 1822, mémorandum de Castlereagh de mai 1820, mort de Castlereagh en août 1822 et arrivée de Canning, intervention française en Espagne en 1823, doctrine Monroe de décembre 1823, reconnaissance britannique des États latino-américains en 1824-25, bataille de Navarin en octobre 1827). Le sujet situe la fin du système « dans les années 1820 » : la discussion distingue l'effondrement des congrès (1822) de la persistance du Concert. Aucun chiffre avancé.

questions.enonce_markdown:
To what do you attribute the demise of the Congress System in Europe in the 1820s?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The Congress System (also called the Concert of Europe) was the arrangement by which the great powers (Britain, Russia, Austria and Prussia, joined by France in 1818) agreed after the Napoleonic Wars to meet in congresses to maintain the territorial settlement of Vienna (1815) and to deal with threats to peace. It was founded on the Quadruple Alliance of November 1815, renewed at the end of the occupation of France, and was linked to the Holy Alliance of Russia, Austria and Prussia, which was based on conservative and religious principles. It held congresses at Aix-la-Chapelle (1818), Troppau (1820), Laibach (1821) and Verona (1822), but after 1822 regular congresses ceased. This collapse is attributed mainly to the different aims of Britain and the eastern powers, to the revolutions in Spain, Italy, Latin America and Greece, to the policies of individual statesmen and to the practical difficulties of the system.

**1. The divergence between Britain and the continental powers.**
- Britain, with its parliamentary government and trade interests, was reluctant to use the alliance to suppress revolutions and defend monarchies in other countries. Castlereagh stated in his State Paper of May 1820 that the Quadruple Alliance was meant to prevent French aggression, not to interfere in the internal affairs of other states. Austria (Metternich), Russia (Alexander I) and Prussia held that the allies had a right and a duty to intervene against revolution, as set out in the Troppau Protocol of 1820.
- This disagreement widened after the revolutions in Spain (1820), Naples (1820) and Piedmont (1821). Britain refused to join in authorising Austrian intervention, though Austrian troops crushed the Neapolitan and Piedmontese revolts in 1821.

**2. The Spanish question and the Congress of Verona (1822).** When France proposed to intervene in Spain to restore Ferdinand VII, Britain, now represented by Wellington as Castlereagh had died in August 1822, refused to approve and left the Congress. George Canning, the new Foreign Secretary, followed a policy of non-intervention and British national interest. The French army invaded Spain in 1823 and restored Ferdinand, but without British support; this showed that the alliance had ceased to be united.

**3. Latin America.** The Spanish colonies in America had been fighting for independence since about 1810; Britain wished to trade with them and eventually recognised the independence of several states in 1824-25 (Canning said he had "called the New World into existence to redress the balance of the Old"). The United States, in the Monroe Doctrine (December 1823), declared opposition to new European colonisation in the Americas and to intervention. These policies defied the Holy Alliance's plan to help Spain recover its colonies and made it clear that the congress principle could not be applied outside Europe.

**4. The Greek revolt (1821-30).** The Greek rising against the Ottoman Empire divided the powers: Metternich, who feared that any national revolution would endanger the order, and Alexander I, who sympathised with fellow Orthodox Christians and wished to expand Russian influence in the Balkans, took opposite sides, and Britain was concerned about Russian influence in the Mediterranean. The attempt to deal with the problem by conference (St Petersburg, 1824-25) failed. Eventually Britain, France and Russia, against Austria's wishes, intervened to help Greece (the Treaty of London of July 1827 and the destruction of the Ottoman-Egyptian fleet at Navarino in October 1827), and Greece became independent after Russia's war with Turkey (1828-29); the powers acting together here showed that the concert survived in a different form, but not in the form of the congresses.

**5. Other factors.**
- *Personal and political changes.* Castlereagh's death in 1822 and the arrival of Canning (who disliked congress diplomacy and preferred direct national policy), the death of Alexander I in 1825 and the increasing influence of Metternich and the conservative powers all weakened cooperation. Alexander's own shift from liberal ideas to conservatism after 1820 made the cooperation between the eastern powers closer, but it widened the gap with Britain.
- *Rise of nationalism and liberalism.* The forces of nationalism and liberalism, which the Vienna settlement had suppressed, produced revolutions in many countries and made the preservation of the status quo by congress impossible to maintain in the long term.
- *Mistrust and national rivalry.* Each power gave priority to its own interests: Russia in the Balkans, Austria in Italy, France in Spain, Britain in trade, and the system did not have a permanent organisation, an army or a commonly accepted principle.

**6. Assessment.** The break-up was therefore mainly due to the difference between the principle of intervention held by the eastern powers and Britain's policy of non-intervention, which became unavoidable once questions arose (Spain, Latin America, Greece) which affected the interests of the powers in different ways. Nevertheless, the habit of consultation between the great powers did not entirely vanish, and conferences were used for the Greek and Belgian questions in the later 1820s and 1830.

**Conclusion.** The Congress System collapsed in the 1820s mainly because the powers could not agree on a common policy toward revolutions: Britain's rejection of intervention, backed by its commercial interests and by Castlereagh and Canning, clashed with the conservative intervention of Austria, Russia and Prussia. The revolutions in Spain, Italy, Latin America and Greece, the rival interests of individual states and changes in leadership made the system unworkable, although the principle of great power consultation survived in a looser form.
